newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish parties agree balanced 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Danish parties agree balanced 1997 budget.

text.p: Denmark's minority government and opposition Conservatives on Thursday held lengthy negotiations to try to agree on a draft 1997 budget.
"We'll thrash it out for as long as there is the prospect of a result, whether positive or negative," Finance Minister Mogens Lykketoft told reporters during a break in talks.
But he said there was no disagreement on the Conservatives' request to reduce the forecast public sector deficit of 5.8 billion danish crowns ($999 million) to zero.
"It has been the point of departure all along that we should do that," he said.
He would not say what he was prepared to offer nor what the Conservatives were demanding but said a cut in corporation tax would probably be on the agenda.
Newspaper reports say the government will propose a cut to 28 percent from its present 34 percent, financed by a tax on shares held as part of pension schemes.
The cost to planholders of the new levy will be offset by an overall rise in share values resulting from business activity stimulated by the cut in corporation tax, analysts say.

Political sources say that the main sticking points are likely to be over other taxes, with the Conservatives demanding, and likely to get, a reduction in the two percent levy that owner-occupiers pay on the estimated value of living in their own property rather than paying rent.
But they will be hard put to accept a likely proposal to raise the gross rate of income tax from its present eight percent to 12 percent over a three-year period.
Conservative leader Hans Engell gave nothing away during the evening. "We are talking and that is positive," he said.
The talks which began at 0930 GMT and went on throughout the day resumed at 2130 GMT after a break for internal discussions on each side.

It is a Danish political tradition, born of successive minority governments, that the ruling coalition seeks to win a consensus on its budget proposals with the main opposition parties before submitting the package to parliament.

Until last year the tradition included a joint front by the Conservatives and their erstwhile Liberal allies but in the 1996 horse-trading Engell surprised Danes -- and Liberal leader Uffe Ellemann-Jensen -- by negotiating a separate deal.
The Liberals, the largest opposition party but increasingly marginalised by Conservative co-operattion with the Social Democrat-led government, were left to sign on to the 1996 budget afterward.
Lykketoft on Thursday said that he had not discussed with the Conservatives whether any agreement the two sides might reach this year should also be put to the Liberals. ($1=5.805 Danish Crown)
